articles.title: Christopher Saunders: Former Australian bishop jailed for sexually abusing young men
articles.summary: The former Bishop of Broome is one of the most senior Catholic clerics in the world to face sex abuse charges.
articles.body:
Former Australian bishop Christopher Saunders has been jailed for sexually abusing two young Aboriginal men during his time as a Catholic cleric.

Saunders - who resigned as Bishop of Broome when first accused of wrongdoing in 2020 - was found guilty of one charge of rape and 12 counts of indecent assault in August.

The 76-year-old was on Wednesday sentenced to six and a half years in prison, but will be eligible for release on parole in February 2031.

He is one of the most senior Catholic leaders in the world to face sex abuse charges.

His trial in the state of Western Australia heard Saunders systematically groomed the two young men, inviting them to "shirts-off" gatherings and plying them with alcohol, often using church funds and church-owned properties to do so.

He was convicted of kissing and molesting the men between 2010 and 2019, and in one instance forcing oral sex on one of them.

In a victim impact statement provided to the court, that young man said he still struggled to talk about what had happened.

"I was a toy that he was using," the victim wrote. "My head is pounding now, I'm in so much pain."

"I trusted him. I thought he wanted me to be a better person."

During the trial several child sex abuse charges were discarded, and Saunders was acquitted by the jury of alleged offences against a third young man.

First ordained in 1976, Saunders spent most of his career in the remote Kimberley region in the nation's north-west corner, and was appointed Bishop of Broome in 1996.

The diocese stretches about 770,000 sq km (297,000 sq miles) - an area roughly the size of Turkey - and encompasses some of the most remote parts of the country.

District Court Judge Martin Flynn said Saunders had professed to be an advocate for young Aboriginal men, but instead misused his authority and exploited their vulnerability.

He had "disregarded the dignity" of his victims and caused them lasting harm.

In a statement, Archbishop of Perth Timothy Costelloe said the men who had come forward had shown great courage and resilience in pursuing justice.

"We are sorry for the pain and suffering that was inflicted on you. We are sorry that your trust was so directly and profoundly betrayed by a leader of the church," he said.

"No court sentence can undo the suffering that has been caused or restore all that each person has lost."

The accusations were first aired in 2020, but the initial police investigation that followed was closed without charge.

However after a historic inquiry was ordered by the Pope, police began a new investigation.

Costelloe has previously said the church's investigation into Saunders - paused when police resumed theirs - will restart.

The church is under pressure to strip Saunders of his remaining title and ministry powers, a decision the Archbishop said would be determined by Rome.

Only a handful of "Vos Estis Lux Mundi" - meaning "You Are the Light of the World" in Latin - inquiries have been undertaken around the world.

The investigations are commissioned by the pontiff and were introduced in 2019 to combat sexual abuse and hold bishops and other high-ranking Catholic Church officials accountable for their actions.

Aside from the late Cardinal George Pell, who was jailed and then acquitted, Saunders is the most senior Catholic official in the country to be charged with sex offences.

articles.title: Oracle donates $10 million to Nashville Symphony; gets thanks note for saving jobs; says: This gift from Oracle is a profound vote of...
articles.summary: Oracle has given $10 million to the Nashville Symphony, a week after the orchestra suspended its 2026/27 season and said it would furlough every one of
articles.body: Oracle has given $10 million to the Nashville Symphony, a week after the orchestra suspended its 2026/27 season and said it would furlough every one of its musicians. The amount matches the shortfall to the dollar. When the symphony shut the season down, it disclosed a $10 million operating-budget deficit for the fiscal year.The symphony confirmed the gift in a letter to patrons on October 4, saying the season will resume and the furloughs will not go ahead. "This gift from Oracle is a profound vote of confidence in the Nashville Symphony and the important role we play in the cultural fabric of our city," wrote Mark Tillinger, the symphony's president and CEO. The season runs through June 2027.Oracle's donation saves jobs for 77 musicians and 27 staffersThe furloughs were due to begin on October 18 and would have covered all 77 members of the orchestra along with 27 full-time staff. Oracle CEO Clay Magouyrk said the donation allows the symphony to bring all of them back."We are here to help solve the community's problems and ensure Nashville remains a vibrant place to live and work for generations to come," he said. The company is building its new headquarters in the city.According to Tillinger, it was the tech giant that made the first move, asking how it could make "a real, meaningful difference". "We shared what it would take to bring our season and our musicians back, and Oracle met that moment with extraordinary vision and generosity," he said.Ticket holders affected by the cancellations will receive an email with their options. Some concerts are still being reconfirmed, depending on whether guest conductors and artists are available on the original dates.Nashville Symphony's money troubles came with a sudden leadership changeThe crisis surfaced on September 28, when the symphony announced the suspension. "The organization has exhausted its cash and cannot continue operating as it has," then CEO J. Mark Cantrell said at the time.Cantrell stepped down days later, about two months into the job. The board replaced him with Tillinger, a former board member. The symphony has not explained why Cantrell left.Oracle's gift buys time while the symphony restructures its financesTillinger has not presented the money as the end of the problem. He said the symphony will now take on "the difficult but necessary work of restructuring our operations, bringing our costs and revenue into balance." He also told patrons that support from individuals, businesses and community partners remains essential.Nashville is not the only orchestra in this position. Ensembles across the US are still dealing with the after-effects of the pandemic, which sped up the decline of season-ticket subscriptions and left them leaning harder on donors. Last month, Cleveland Orchestra musicians went on a three-day strike over wages, and a strike at the San Francisco Opera cost it its season opener. The Boston Symphony has been in turmoil since it chose not to renew music director Andris Nelsons' contract.The Nashville Symphony plays more than 150 concerts a year, with a focus on contemporary American orchestral music, in a city better known for country. Its two biggest fundraisers, the Symphony Ball on December 12 and the Symphony Fashion Show on April 27, 2027, stayed on the calendar even while the concerts were cancelled. How those nights perform will show whether Oracle's $10 million marks the start of a recovery or only rescues this season.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Three new SC judges take oath, all in the name of God; number of women judges in SC – three out of 37
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Three new Supreme Court Judges – Justices Sunita Agarwal, Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Aparesh Kumar Singh – on Tuesday took oath of office in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Three new Supreme Court Judges – Justices Sunita Agarwal, Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Aparesh Kumar Singh – on Tuesday took oath of office in the name of God taking the working strength of SC to 37 judges, just one short of the sanctioned strength.CJI Surya Kant administered oath to Justices Agarwal, Upadhyaya and Singh, who were chief justices of Gujarat, Delhi and Telangana HCs respectively, in the presence of SC judges, attorney general R Venkataramani, solicitor general Tushar Mehta and other senior advocates and lawyers.With the elevation of Justice Agarwal, who is the 13th women judge of SC, the strength of women judges in the apex court at present became three. The other two being Justices B V Nagarathna, who is scheduled to become the first woman CJI on Sep 24 next year, and Justice V Mohana.During the tenure of Justice N V Ramana as CJI, the Supreme Court had the highest number of sitting SC judges at four – Justices India Banerjee, Nagarathna, Hima Kohli and Bela M Trivedi, last three of whom had taken oath on Aug 31, 2021. While the Collegium led by Justice Ramana had recommended appointment of three women judges, the present collegium led by CJI Kant has so far appointed two women judges.SC got its first woman judge in M Fathima Beevi on Oct 6, 1989, 39 years after SC was established. Justice Beevi had retired from Kerala HC on Apr 29, 1989, but was elevated to the SC five months after retirement. Other women judges in SC were – Justices Sujata V Manohar, Ruma Pal, Gyan Sudha Misra, Ranjana P Desai, R Bhanumathi and Indu Malhotra.SC judge strength was increased from 34 to 38, including the CJI, initially through an Ordinance on May 16. The corresponding Amendment Act was passed by Parliament which received the President's assent on Aug 11. In Aug 2019, during the tenure of CJI Ranjan Gogoi, the sanctioned strength of SC judges was increased from 31 to 34, including CJI.The SC had started in 1950 with a sanctioned strength of 8 Judges, which was increased to 11 in 1956, 14 in 1960, 18 in 1978, 26 in 1986, and 31 in 2009. articles.title: Omani pilot had failed airline stints, flydubai hired him in post-pandemic spree: Report
articles.summary: Omani pilot who allegedly tried to crash a flydubai jet on a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight had failed stints with airlines in Oman and Morocco before being hired
articles.body: Omani pilot who allegedly tried to crash a flydubai jet on a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight had failed stints with airlines in Oman and Morocco before being hired by the carrier as a part of "rapid post-pandemic recruitment drive", Wall Street Journal reported.The 29-year-old pilot, identified as Hamam al-Hammami, joined flydubai in February as the airline was rapidly rebuilding its workforce after the pandemic. The recruitment of the pilot has now come under scrutiny following the attempted crash.Flydubai has built its network around destinations that some Western carriers have avoided because of security or operational challenges. The airline operates routes to places including Kabul and Damascus, and continued flying to Tel Aviv even after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, when several other carriers suspended services.Its staff strength nearly doubled from 3,682 in 2021 to 6,763 by the end of 2025. Its pilot numbers also rose to about 1,500 from 658 a decade earlier, according to company figures, the report said.The airline had stepped up recruitment as air travel recovered, conducting hiring drives and expanding pilot training and cadet programmes.The first officer allegedly attacked the captain with an axe during the flight in an attempt to bring down the Boeing aircraft. The attempt failed and the plane did not crash. Flydubai said it was cooperating with investigators following the incident.“The safety and wellbeing of our passengers, crew and operations remain our highest priority,” the airline said.The Dubai-Tel Aviv route has been suspended since the incident.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'I asked for Rs 600, they paid me Rs 300': How payment dispute turned deadly for elderly couple, house help in Dehradun
articles.summary: DEHRADUN: An 80-year-old retired works manager at an ordnance factory in Dehradun was allegedly murdered along with his wife and their house help at their
articles.body: DEHRADUN: An 80-year-old retired works manager at an ordnance factory in Dehradun was allegedly murdered along with his wife and their house help at their home on Tuesday.Police arrested Raj Kumar, a plumber from Uttar Pradesh’s Bijnor who had been working in Dehradun for around five years, in connection with the killings.The victims were identified as Ramesh Kapoor, his wife Rajni, 75, and their house help Tilya Devi, 48. Police said all three were stabbed with a screwdriver.Plumber called for repair workDehradun SSP Pramendra Dobal said Kumar told police that he had been called to the Kapoors’ home in the Raipur area for plumbing work.According to the SSP, Kumar had carried out plumbing jobs for the couple in the past. After completing the work on Tuesday, he allegedly argued with Kapoor over payment.“Hearing the commotion, house help Tilya tried to stop Raj Kumar but he stabbed her too with a screwdriver...” Dobal said.Police said Kumar then allegedly fled with a gold chain belonging to the couple.Neighbours chased man in blood-stained clothesVishal Rana, a neighbour who took the victims to hospital, said the incident took place around 2.30pm.“We saw a man hastily walking away in the blood stained clothes. Locals chased him and caught him. A screwdriver was found near the victims which is believed to be the murder weapon,” Rana said.Police said Kumar was subsequently arrested and an FIR was registered against him under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita’s murder provision on a complaint by Tilya’s family.Accused cites payment disputeSpeaking to reporters, Kumar claimed the dispute was over the amount he was paid for the plumbing work.“I asked for Rs 600, they were paying me Rs 300, so I stabbed them with screwdriver,” he said.Couple’s sons live in Pune, DelhiThe Kapoors had two sons, who live in Pune and Delhi. Tilya, who was from Bihar, was the mother of four children.Police are examining the evidence recovered from the house and questioning Kumar as part of the investigation.Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news. articles.title: Hampshire woman wants to break silence on medical terminations
articles.summary: Rosanna Brown was advised to end her pregnancy because her baby had a life-threatening condition.
articles.body:
A woman whose baby was too ill to be born is calling for better awareness of choosing a termination for medical reasons.

Rosanna Brown, who lives near Waterlooville, Hampshire, was advised to end her pregnancy with son William in 2023 because he had a rare and life-threatening medical condition called Chaos syndrome.

Continuing the pregnancy would have risked both their lives, but Rosanna said the experience was made even more difficult due to a lack of training around medically-advised abortions.

An NHS spokesperson said it offered "comprehensive support for women whose unborn baby is diagnosed with a serious health condition".

Rosanna said she understood why so many people who suffered a termination for medical reasons (TFMR) just told others they had had a miscarriage.

"Because it's a type of abortion, you have the pro-life pro-choice argument, you are thrown into the middle of that," she said.

"You have this feeling that your grief isn't as valid because you've chosen [it].

"It's such a complex and lonely thing to go through and it's so much harder if you can't tell the truth of what happened to you.

"Because for so many parents, termination is the most loving thing they could offer."

About 5,000 women a year are offered a TFMR, which is more than experience stillbirth and neonatal death.

Rosanna is campaigning for change, including for the term TFMR to be properly used, which she said it was not on her son's forms.

Instead her loss was described as a "late miscarriage", which she said "silences you further".

"I made a choice here, I didn't naturally lose my baby," she said.

"I didn't come across [TFMR] until a good few months after I'd lost him. And in that time, you're searching for community and for support and for compassion for people to get it.

"And if that term is not being used by medical professionals with the patients that they're seeing, I think sometimes it's because they're worried about offending you."

Jane Fisher, chief executive of the ARC Charity, said it was a very difficult situation and that using the right term was really important.

"It describes the reality of the situation and I think that's important both for parents to accept what happened but also for us to break the stigma and taboo around this particular loss," she said.

She added without that, it could be "very difficult to grieve in a healthy way".

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "Every woman going through this incredibly difficult situation deserves proper care, compassion and support."

They added: "All major abortion providers offer counselling and advice on the options available."

A NHS spokesperson also said it provided mental health support for baby loss following a decision to terminate a pregnancy.

Earlier this year, Rosanna and her husband became parents again to a daughter.

But they said they would always talk about her big brother William and had planted a memorial garden in his honour.

Ahead of Baby Loss Awareness Week, she has written and published a compassionate guide to help others, called The Silence Of TFMR.

She said: "Some of the most painful advice [was] 'don't let this define you'. I really took offence because your identity changes, your whole life changes.

"I am defined [by it] and am quite happy to be. I need to find ways to keep tapping into that identity of parent to him because that's the only way he gets to exist, in this world."

Baby Loss Awareness Week takes place from 9 to 15 October.

articles.title: Dead seabird tests carried out after Port of Tyne nurdle spill
articles.summary: Necropsies are being carried out on seabirds to find out the effects of microplastic pollutants.
articles.body:
Research is being carried out to find out how a microplastic spillage has affected coastal sea bird populations.

On 19 July tonnes of microplastics known as nurdles were spilled into the River Tyne following a collision between ships at the Port of Tyne.

A series of necropsies are now taking place at the Dove Marine Laboratory in Cullercoats on dead birds gathered after the spill.

Dan Turner, coordinator at North East England Beached Bird Surveys said: "We've already seen samples from contents of stomachs of suspected regurgitation which contain nurdles."

Necropsies will be carried out on a variation of seabirds gathered from across the North East including eight guillemots, five herring gulls, a gannet and a pink-footed goose.

The research was prompted over concerns birds could "starve" if they confuse the nurdles for food and fill their stomachs.

"We've seen evidence previously of fulmars eating plastic and they've been found in their stomachs, so it is highly likely we could come across the same in some cases," Turner added.

Charities like the RSPB have also warned the pellets could enter the wider food chain, affecting fish, seals and dolphins.

External and internal studies into the seabirds has started with stomach rinsing also taking place to see if the birds have been consuming the nurdles.

"It is quite possible that the seabirds have mistaken the plastic for fish eggs.

"The nurdles when they float attract pollutants and contaminants, which stick to them, if the birds swallow them it can be the case that they get into the bird's system.

"We may need more testing to see if the plastic can make its way into the bird's bloodstream which could cause a drop in the bird's fitness," Turner said.

Researchers have confirmed 28% of 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles which spilled into the river have been recovered since the spill.

Scientists predict that the plastic pellets will continue to wash up on North East beaches as the clean up continues.

Colin Porter who has been assisting the clean up in South Tyneside said: "We are very concerned about the wildlife populations, we've seen birds eating them and we know the fish have too."

The research on the birds is expected to continue into December.

articles.title: From Shakti to Aravalli: India's helicopter engine journey takes shape
articles.summary: Defence minister Rajnath Singh has inaugurated a second production line for Shakti helicopter engines at Hindustan Aeronautics Limited's Koraput division,
articles.body: Defence minister Rajnath Singh has inaugurated a second production line for Shakti helicopter engines at Hindustan Aeronautics Limited's Koraput division, an event that also marked the delivery of the facility's 2,000th aero-engine. The Rs 218 crore facility, expected to be fully operational by 2028-29, will produce up to 100 Shakti engines annually, powering indigenous platforms including the Advanced Light Helicopter Dhruv, the Light Combat Helicopter Prachand and the upcoming Light Utility Helicopter. Singh congratulated the engineers, technicians and scientists behind the milestone, calling it a significant moment in India's aerospace journey, and urged that Koraput evolve into a broader aerospace propulsion ecosystem rather than remain focused solely on engine manufacturing.India's helicopter-engine capability has steadily matured over the decades, moving from licensed production of foreign engines towards genuine joint development and, increasingly, indigenous design. The Shakti engine, India's version of Safran's Ardiden 1H1, remains the country's most mature modern helicopter-engine programme, jointly developed by HAL and Safran and built for demanding hot-and-high conditions. It currently powers the Dhruv, Rudra and Prachand. This builds on earlier experience with licensed production of the Artouste III B for the Chetak and Cheetah, and later the TM333 for the Cheetal, programmes that strengthened HAL's manufacturing expertise even though the core designs remained foreign.The next step up is the Aravalli, a more powerful 3,500 to 4,000 shp turboshaft engine being jointly developed through HAL and Safran's 50:50 SAFHAL venture, with a final development and production contract signed in August 2026. The Aravalli is intended for the Indian Multi-Role Helicopter and the naval Deck-Based Multi-Role Helicopter, pushing India into a higher engine power class altogether. Separately, HAL's Aero Engine Research and Development Centre is working on the HTSE-1200, an effort to develop a genuinely Indian-designed turboshaft for helicopters in the 3.5 to 6.5 tonne class, though this remains at the development stage. India also continues to sustain foreign engines domestically, including the TM333 and the GE T700 used on Apache helicopters, without manufacturing them locally.Established in 1964, the Koraput division has a long legacy of powering frontline aircraft including the MiG-21, MiG-27, MiG-29 and Su-30MKI, and has overhauled more than 9,000 engines over the years. Singh also announced that HAL would raise its annual production capacity of AL-31FP engines for the Su-30MKI from 30 to 50 units, backed by an investment of Rs 335 crore. Against a 2024 order for 240 engines, HAL has already delivered 63, exceeding its second-year target of 60 despite ongoing supply-chain and raw-material challenges.The defence minister described the aero-engine as the heart of any aircraft, stressing that propulsion mastery is essential to fully exploit advanced airframes, weapons, radars and avionics. He underlined the importance of indigenous capability in superalloys, advanced materials, precision manufacturing and testing, and linked this propulsion push directly to the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft programme, citing a proposed investment of around Rs 5,000 crore, indigenous raw-material development with MIDHANI, and the establishment of India's first indigenous high-thrust engine testing facility.

articles.title: In 2003, a New York woman pulled a painting from trash on Manhattan’s Upper West Side; four years later she learned it was a stolen Rufino Tamayo work, and Sotheby’s sold it for $1,049,000
articles.summary: In 2003, Elizabeth Gibson was taking a morning walk on Manhattan’s Upper West Side when she noticed a brightly coloured abstract painting lying in the
articles.body: In 2003, Elizabeth Gibson was taking a morning walk on Manhattan’s Upper West Side when she noticed a brightly coloured abstract painting lying in the trash. She did not know who had painted it or why it had been thrown away. Still, something about the work made her stop and take it with her.Gibson later began looking into the painting she had found. Her search eventually led her to the website of “Antiques Roadshow FYI”, a companion programme to the PBS show “Antiques Roadshow”, CBC news reported. That was when she discovered that the painting was not an ordinary piece of discarded artwork.The painting was identified as “Tres Personajes” (Three People), a 1970 work by Mexican artist Rufino Tamayo. It had been bought by a Houston couple at Sotheby’s in 1977 and was stolen from a warehouse in 1987 while the couple were moving.The discovery came four years after Gibson had found the painting. Sotheby’s was preparing to sell the work at its Latin American Art auction on November 20, 2007. The auction house estimated that it could fetch up to $1 million.The 1987 stealingThe Houston couple had bought “Tres Personajes” at Sotheby’s in 1977. The painting is an oil on canvas, with marble dust and sand worked into the paint. According to August Uribe, Sotheby’s senior vice president of Impressionist and modern art, the husband had paid $55,000 for it as a gift for his wife.The painting was kept in a warehouse while the couple were moving. It was stolen from the warehouse in 1987. The couple then reported the theft to Houston and federal authorities.Information about the missing painting was also entered into databases maintained by the International Foundation for Art Research and the Art Loss Register. Despite those efforts, there were no credible leads about where the work had gone.The painting eventually turned up in a completely different setting. Gibson found it lying in rubbish on a street in Manhattan, apparently unaware that it was a valuable work that had been missing for years.For Gibson, the discovery was not simply about finding an unusual painting. She said she immediately felt that the artwork had some importance, even though she did not understand why.“I would say it was an appointment with destiny,” Gibson said in a telephone interview with the Los Angeles Times. “I just knew it meant something. It was extremely powerful, and even though I didn’t understand it. I knew it had power,” she added.Discovering the identityGibson's search for information about the painting eventually connected her to “Antiques Roadshow FYI”. Uribe had featured “Tres Personajes” on the programme’s “Missing Masterpieces” segment.That helped Gibson realise that the painting she had taken from the rubbish was the same work that had been stolen from the Houston couple two decades earlier.By then, Tamayo's work had become highly valuable. Sotheby’s described “Tres Personajes” as an important work from the artist’s mature period and prepared it for the upcoming auction.The original owner, whose husband had since died, was putting the painting up for sale. The couple had also offered a $15,000 reward for information leading to the recovery of the stolen work.Gibson was due to receive that $15,000 reward. She was also set to receive an undisclosed percentage of the eventual sale price.Rufino Tamayo and ‘Tres Personajes’Tamayo was born in 1899 in the Mexican state of Oaxaca. He studied at Mexico’s School of Fine Arts and began his career with work that had similarities to the style of well-known Mexican muralists such as Diego Rivera.His later work became more individual. It included vivid colours and expressions associated with Oaxaca, along with influences from pre-Columbian art.“Tres Personajes” reflected this later period of his career. Sotheby’s considered the 1970 painting an important example of Tamayo’s mature work.Tamayo became internationally known during his lifetime. He received numerous prizes and exhibited his work in the United States, South America, Europe and Russia. He died in 1991, but his paintings continued to attract strong interest.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1992, Larry Ellison shattered his elbow in a bicycle crash; after a UC Davis surgeon repaired it, the Oracle co-founder gave $5 million to help others with bone and muscle disorders
articles.summary: A serious bicycle accident suffered by Oracle CEO Larry Ellison in the early 1990s ultimately resulted in a $5 million donation that helped expand
articles.body: A serious bicycle accident suffered by Oracle CEO Larry Ellison in the early 1990s ultimately resulted in a $5 million donation that helped expand research into bone and muscle disorders at UC Davis, according to the university. The Oracle co-founder's gift helped build a musculoskeletal research and care program at UC Davis that is still part of the university's orthopaedic identity. Ellison, the co-founder and longtime chief executive of Oracle, shattered his elbow in a bicycle crash in 1992. The injury was treated by Michael Chapman, an orthopaedic surgeon at UC Davis, who successfully reconstructed the damaged joint. Following the surgery, Ellison donated $5 million to support musculoskeletal research and patient care at the university.The gift helped establish what became the Lawrence J. Ellison Musculoskeletal Research Center, where physicians, surgeons and scientists work on research aimed at preventing and treating musculoskeletal disorders. According to UC Davis, the centre focuses on conditions affecting bones, muscles and joints, bringing together experts from multiple disciplines.Record-setting donation made by Larry EllisonUC Davis announced the pledge in September 1995, when it reported record private giving of $41.5 million for fiscal year 1994-95. That was a 39 percent increase over the $29.8 million raised the year before. Ellison, then CEO of Oracle, made the largest single gift of the year. The $5 million pledge was meant to create three endowed chairs and a musculoskeletal institute in the School of Medicine."Mr. Ellison's generosity in particular will help sustain our nationally recognized expertise and care for patients with bone or muscle diseases," said Gerald S. Lazarus, then dean of the School of Medicine. The School of Medicine received $12.7 million in private support that year, an 88 percent increase. The university said this was the largest amount ever given to an academic unit on the campus.What the money builtThe Ellison center brings together physicians, surgeons and basic scientists. They study the prevention and treatment of what UC Davis calls "crippling and painful musculoskeletal disorders."A 2011 UC Davis Health profile described the center as part of a broader orthopaedic and sports medicine program. Its specialists have served as team doctors for the NBA's Sacramento Kings for more than two decades. The same program provides care for Olympic-level athletes, the national soccer program and UC Davis teams. US News & World Report ranked UC Davis among the nation's best hospitals for orthopaedics.Paul Di Cesare, then chair of orthopaedic surgery, said the program uses the same advanced techniques for professionals and ordinary patients. "We use those same modalities and treatments for the average athlete and the weekend warrior," he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Those who opposed me taught me power of democracy': PM Modi on completing 25 years in public service - top quotes
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday addressed the ‘Viksit Bharat Sankalp Sabha’ programme organised to mark 25 years of his public
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday addressed the ‘Viksit Bharat Sankalp Sabha’ programme organised to mark 25 years of his public service, first as Gujarat chief minister and later as the country’s prime minister. People welcomed PM Modi on his arrival by showering flowers, waving BJP flags and chanting ‘Bharat Mata ki Jai’.The Prime Minister attributed his political journey to the faith and support of the people, and expressed gratitude to citizens as well as his colleagues in the National Democratic Alliance (NDA).Addressing the gathering in the presence of PM Modi, BJP president Nitin Nabin congratulated the prime minister on completing 25 years as head of government.Here are the top quotes:Today, I have completed 25 years of continuously serving as Head of Government. This is the blessing of the people. I bow before the people of the country.On October 7, 2001, when I took the oath as the Chief Minister of Gujarat, I had not imagined that this milestone, too, would arrive.The people have always chosen me to serve them. Today, I pay tribute to India's democracy and its Constitution. I also extend my heartfelt appreciation to all the citizens participating in the 'Seva Jyoti Yatra'. This morning I visited the Sri Vinayaka Temple to offer prayers. I prayed to the Almighty for the nation—for the 1.4 billion people of India—and for myself as well. My prayer was that the Almighty grant me the strength and capability to work for my country with even greater energy.Whatever I am today, wherever I stand, and in whatever role I serve, the biggest contribution belongs to the 'janata janardhan.' For me, the public is a manifestation of God itself. The trust of hundreds of millions of countrymen and the tireless effort of millions of party workers has been my greatest strength.Those who stood by me showed me power of faith, those who opposed me taught me power of democracy.Viksit Bharat by 2047, we will do it! Aatmanirbhar bharat! Global Manufacturing hub! Hosting of the Olympics! Stepping into Space! This energy and confidence are incredible.I sincerely believe that every citizen of India has foremost claim on me. I have been a person who has lived for a mission, not my personal ambition. I have never felt alone; there are countless 'swayamsevaks' who are guardians of India's cultural soul.I remember when I used to attend school in Vadnagar, our teacher would impart various lessons, and my name was always among those students who reached the classroom first. That eagerness to learn became an integral part of my life, and even today, I consider myself a lifelong student. I attempt to learn something new every single day. The more I learn, the greater my ability to contribute to the nation will grow. When I look back today, I am filled only with a sense of deep gratitude.25 years ago, at the age of 50, I had spent my time serving tribal communities in the forests and living amidst the mountains, eventually choosing the path of organizational work within the Bharatiya Janata Party. My political report card reflected only the work of an organizational worker. I had been involved in elections, yet I had never contested one myself. Had I desired to shine in electoral politics, I could have entered the arena long ago; but that was not my temperament.One of the major tragedies our country has faced is that, for the sake of politics, society was divided along the lines of votes. Think about it... if water does not reach a field, who suffers? Is it only farmers from one caste who are affected? If there is no electricity, does darkness prevail only in the homes of one community? The answer to all these questions is no. If the problem is everyone’s, then the solution should also be for everyone. That is why we linked good governance with saturation. Saturation means every eligible beneficiary is covered, no deserving person is left out, no one is deprived of their rightful benefits, and no one can take away another person’s rights. That is saturation. That is the real story of change.Our country has problems, but we also have 140 crore solutions. This is not the time to rest. This is the time to move forward with determination and enthusiasm, to devote ourselves completely to the service of the nation. The fact that India is so young today, with such a large young population, is a tremendous opportunity given to us by history. We must not let this opportunity slip away.Today the country is finding permanent solutions to its challenges. The issue of Article 370 in Jammu and Kashmir once seemed endless, with the country seemingly unable to escape its adverse effects; yet today, the wall of Article 370 has been completely demolished. Similarly, the problem of Naxalism was once considered a national curse, but today, its backbone has been broken. Terrorism was challenging India's very destiny. Citizens had come to believe that neither the terrorists nor their masters would ever relent. But such is India's indomitable will—we struck them down right inside their own strongholds.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Dawn Chaney was a three-sport athlete at Texas Woman's University in the 1960s; decades later, she gave $10 million for a new athletics complex
articles.summary: Dawn Chaney’s connection with Texas Woman’s University began as a student-athlete in the 1960s and has now grown into one of the university’s largest
articles.body: Dawn Chaney’s connection with Texas Woman’s University began as a student-athlete in the 1960s and has now grown into one of the university’s largest philanthropic legacies. A three-sport competitor during her time at TWU, Chaney later built a career in higher education and real estate. In 2026, she committed $10 million towards a new athletics complex that will carry her name. The approximately $30 million facility is expected to break ground in 2027, giving the university a new space designed around the needs of its growing athletics programme.What shaped Dawn Chaney’s connection with Texas Woman’s University Chaney’s relationship with Texas Woman’s University stretches across three degrees and several decades. According to TWU’s Pioneer Scholarship System, she is a three-time alumna of the university and earned degrees connected with kinesiology. The university’s July 2026 announcement also notes that she was a three-sport athlete during the 1960s, making her later support for athletics closely connected to her own experience as a student.Her professional life eventually moved beyond sport. As reported by TWU in 2022, Chaney spent 17 years teaching in higher education, working at institutions including Texas A&I University, the State University of New York, the University of Delaware and Bennett College in Greensboro, North Carolina. She later entered real estate investment and developed Chaney Properties.Her career became a foundation for philanthropyChaney’s work in property development grew from a single-family property she acquired when she started Chaney Properties in 1980, according to the university’s scholarship profile. The business later expanded into single-family, multi-family, commercial, industrial and warehouse properties, with a particular focus on historic properties around downtown Greensboro.Her connection with TWU also remained active. The university’s 2022 report states that Chaney gave $100,000 to establish two $50,000 scholarship endowments for undergraduate and graduate students. The awards were intended to support students studying exercise physiology and exercise science, as well as students committed to women’s leadership.The Pioneer Scholarship System records those as the Dr. Dawn S. Chaney Undergraduate Scholarship Endowment and the Dr. Dawn S. Chaney Graduate Scholarship Endowment. They support students in the School of Health Promotion and Kinesiology, with preference for exercise science students and those demonstrating financial need.What will the new athletics complex provideThe planned facility is designed to address practical pressures created by the growth of TWU athletics. The university says its varsity sports programme expanded from 5 sports to 9 over six years, while the number of student-athletes more than doubled. That growth has placed greater demand on existing training and support spaces.According to TWU’s 2026 announcement, student-athletes currently share Pioneer Hall with academic kinesiology programmes. This has contributed to scheduling conflicts, crowded training areas and limited practice opportunities. Growing teams have also increased demand for locker rooms, weight-training areas and sports medicine facilities.The proposed 30,000- to 35,000-square-foot complex is intended to separate those functions and provide more room for athletes. Planned facilities include an auxiliary practice gym, locker rooms for five teams, a larger weight room capable of accommodating up to 40 athletes at once and a sports medicine clinic staffed by certified athletic trainers.The project reflects a wider rise in Pioneer athleticsThe building is being planned at a time when TWU’s teams have been achieving notable results. The university reports 5 conference championships, 3 regional championships and 5 national championships during the recent period of expansion. Its athletics programme has also received three consecutive conference Academic Excellence Awards, along with the 2025 NCAA Division II President’s Award for Academic Excellence.Community Impact’s report on the planned $30 million facility places the project within this broader expansion of the university’s athletics programme. The new building is intended not only to provide additional training space but also to give the programme room to accommodate future growth.TWU also expects improved facilities to support activities beyond regular competition. The university has identified summer camps, youth programming and community engagement as areas that have been constrained by existing space.Chaney’s wider TWU legacy continues to growThe $10 million athletics gift is not Chaney’s first major contribution to the university. TWU says the new commitment brings her into its top 5 donors and adds to earlier support that includes two kinesiology scholarships, the Chaney West Commons in the Health Sciences Center and founding support for the Texas Woman’s Athletics Hall of Fame.The new athletics complex will bear Chaney’s name as a result of the $10 million commitment, according to TWU. The university expects construction to begin in 2027.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: GE Aerospace shipped four F404-IN20 engines for India’s indigenous Tejas fighter aircraft in September, the company said, as engine availability remains a key factor in Hindustan Aeronautics Limited’s (HAL) production and delivery schedule, news agency ANI reported.The company specifically highlighted its partnership with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and the Indian Air Force, saying it remains focused on delivering the F404-IN20 engines needed for the programme.“GE Aerospace shipped four F404-IN20 engines in September 2026. articles.title: Meet Nick Grewal who received the Entrepreneur of the Year Award; he founded Nashoba Networks, acquired by Cisco in 1996, before building ePropelled, a global propulsion company
articles.summary: More than three decades after entering the technology industry, entrepreneur Nick Grewal has added another distinction to his career: the 2026
articles.body: More than three decades after entering the technology industry, entrepreneur Nick Grewal has added another distinction to his career: the 2026 Entrepreneur of the Year Award from the New Hampshire Tech Alliance, according to a press release by Access Newswire.Grewal, founder, chairman and chief executive officer of ePropelled, was named the recipient of the award in September and formally received it at the Tech Alliance’s Innovation Summit in Nashua on October 6. The recognition follows a career spanning networking technology, investments in high-tech companies, and, more recently, electric propulsion systems for uncrewed vehicles.The New Hampshire Tech Alliance said Grewal has spent more than four decades building companies and advancing emerging technologies. Before turning his attention to autonomous systems, he founded Nashoba Networks, a company that Cisco acquired in 1996. He later founded ePropelled in 2018, taking his career from computer networking into a field focused on electrification, propulsion and autonomous vehicles.Nashoba Networks and the Cisco dealOne of the biggest milestones in Grewal's earlier career came in the 1990s, when he founded Nashoba Networks, a Massachusetts technology company working on Token Ring switching. Cisco's own acquisition records confirm that the company announced an agreement to acquire Nashoba Networks on August 6, 1996. Cisco described Nashoba as a privately held company focused on Token Ring switching technologies and said the acquisition would expand its offerings for high-performance switched workgroup and backbone Token Ring networks.The deal was completed the following month. In a September 19, 1996 announcement, Cisco said it had completed its purchase of Nashoba Networks and that the transaction followed an August stock-swap agreement. According to Cisco, shares worth approximately $100 million were to be exchanged for all outstanding Nashoba shares and options.Grewal subsequently served as a Cisco vice president, according to his profile published by Smart Business Dealmakers. The Nashoba chapter was only one part of a broader technology career. Before and around that period, Grewal held senior executive positions at companies including Proteon and CrossComm, both of which became publicly traded during his tenure, according to the New Hampshire Tech Alliance.From technology investor to another startupAfter the Cisco acquisition, Grewal continued working in technology and investment. Between 1998 and 2018, he invested in and advised more than 40 companies, many of them based in New Hampshire, according to the Tech Alliance. His next major entrepreneurial chapter began in 2018, when he founded ePropelled.The company's original focus was electric vehicle propulsion, with a broader goal of developing highly efficient electrical power, propulsion and energy-management systems. ePropelled says it was founded in Lowell, Massachusetts, in 2018, with Grewal providing the initial private investment.Grewal has led the company as CEO since May 2018, according to ePropelled's leadership profile. The company now develops electric propulsion and energy-management technologies for air, land and water applications, with a particular focus on uncrewed systems.Unlike Nashoba Networks, which operated in the networking technology sector, ePropelled is focused on the growing intersection of electrification and autonomous systems. The New Hampshire Tech Alliance describes the company as designing and manufacturing intelligent propulsion and energy-management systems for uncrewed vehicles operating across air, land and sea. Its technologies are aimed at applications where propulsion efficiency, energy use and system control can affect the performance and endurance of autonomous platforms.The company has expanded beyond its original US base. ePropelled currently has operations, engineering and production facilities in the US, UK and India, according to its investor-relations information. Its UK operations grew after ePropelled acquired ElectronicaUK Ltd in 2018, while its Coventry facility opened in 2022.In 2023, ePropelled moved its headquarters from Massachusetts to Laconia, New Hampshire. The company says it now has more than 40 global customers and develops propulsion products for uncrewed aerial, ground and marine platforms, alongside industrial and other electric-motor applications.Why Grewal received the awardThe Entrepreneur of the Year award is not new. The New Hampshire Tech Alliance says it was first presented in 1988 and recognises technology entrepreneurs based on factors including risk, innovation, growth, competition, profitability and employment.Grewal's selection reflects both his earlier work in networking and his more recent efforts in autonomous and electric systems. The Tech Alliance highlighted his decision to establish ePropelled's headquarters and manufacturing operations in New Hampshire and continue investing in local jobs and facilities as the company grows.His career also illustrates how technology sectors have changed since the 1980s and 1990s. Grewal's first major success was tied to computer networking at a time when businesses were building the infrastructure that would underpin modern internet connectivity. Decades later, his focus has shifted toward systems that combine electric propulsion, energy management and autonomy.Today, ePropelled's work spans aerospace, defence, maritime, industrial and autonomous systems markets. The company says it is developing technologies designed to improve the efficiency, endurance and performance of uncrewed platforms.For Grewal, the latest award marks a new milestone in a career that has already crossed several technology eras: from networking hardware and a Cisco acquisition in the 1990s to electric propulsion and autonomous vehicles in the 2020s.You use AI every day. articles.title: Delhi Police yet to give CJP permission for October 10 protest; Saurav Das asks, ‘Who are they to deny it?’
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convenor Saurav Das on Wednesday submitted a formal notice to the Delhi Police informing them about the party's
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convenor Saurav Das on Wednesday submitted a formal notice to the Delhi Police informing them about the party's proposed October 10 protest at Jantar Mantar, where it plans to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Das submitted the letter at Parliament Street police station, saying the party had formally informed the police to avoid any dispute later over whether authorities had been notified about the demonstration.He said the CJP would cooperate with the police during the protest and expected the police to do the same.However, police officials are yet to give permission for the proposed protest on October 10.Addressing the media, Das said, “We reached the Parliament Street Police Station, and I handed them a formal letter. We informed them that the 'Cockroach Janta Party' and the youth of the entire nation, all these 'cockroaches’, are set to gather at Jantar Mantar on October 10. We asked them to maintain law and order, cooperate with us, and make necessary traffic arrangements. We have provided this formal intimation.”He said the Delhi Police acknowledged the formal notification and that they had also submitted an undertaking and completed the required formalities.“We have submitted the formal notification and have received the acknowledgement copy from the Delhi Police. Based on our discussions, they also obtained an undertaking from us, and we completed all the required formalities for it. We hope the Delhi Police will cooperate,” he said.Questioning the need for police “permission” for a protest at a designated demonstration site, Das said the police's role should be to ensure the safety of protesters, maintain law and order and regulate traffic rather than decide whether citizens could protest.“Jantar Mantar is a designated protest site and a historic place where protests are held peacefully,” Das said.He also launched a sharp attack on Kumar, calling the CEC a “traitor” and “anti-national” and making allegations about his conduct.The October 10 protest was announced by CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke after the party's October 2 demonstration at Mumbai's Shivaji Park. Dipke had said CJP activists from across the country would march to Delhi if Kumar did not resign.CJP alleges activists being pressuredThe Delhi protest comes amid allegations by Dipke that CJP activists in Maharashtra were being pressured not to attend the agitation.At a press conference in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar on Tuesday, Dipke alleged that Chandrapur police had issued notices to CJP workers, questioning them about the source of funds for their travel to Delhi and asking them not to participate in the October 10 protest.He also questioned how police could know in advance that the proposed agitation would turn violent.The CJP has been protesting against alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise and demanding Kumar's resignation. articles.title: Rainmakers: Will drones make cloud seeding more effective?
articles.summary: Cloud seeding is gaining attention as countries look to boost rainfall - will drones help?
articles.body:
On 23 August, Cooper Freeman had no idea clouds above his head were being filled with a silver compound in order to cause rainfall.

Neither did thousands of other residents in Homer, Alaska, who later discovered San Francisco start-up Rainmaker conducted an experiment in that region using cloud-seeding technology.

The company claims it produced 19 million US gallons of water in the sky in three hours.

This approach to weather modification, now more than 80-years-old, involves using planes and drones to disperse compounds such as silver iodide into clouds to form ice crystals. Those crystals eventually become large enough to fall as rain or snow, depending on the temperatures below.

Essentially, cloud seeding speeds up the natural process of water vapor condensing inside of clouds. Gravity then pulls those crystals to the ground. The technology, though, needs ideal climate environments, such as mountainous or cold regions such as Alaska.

Freeman, the Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, isn't just concerned Homer residents weren't widely alerted to these experiments. He's sceptical about what was shot into the clouds, and questions how safe it was for both residents and their habitat.

"It doesn't appear that there was any downstream monitoring to verify that this silver iodide didn't impact the environment," he says.

Freeman adds, "Having a company come in to do this seeding isn't going to solve our water woes, and it feels like a distraction from solving the urgent issues related to water conservation."

Concerns are mounting about the challenges surrounding water security. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in July "our world is using freshwater faster than it can be replenished ", which echoes reports noting how the past five years have led to the driest period for global rivers in more than three decades.

Cloud-seeding technology may be a drop in the bucket, as it doesn't create rainstorms. For example, Rainmaker's 19 million gallons equates to around 0.01 inch of rain across 100 square miles.

Nevertheless, more than 50 countries are developing programmes to modify the weather and a surge of start-ups are developing systems to create rain.

As well developed and promising as this innovative field has become, these businesses continue to face thorny questions on safety and efficacy, leading to novel approaches with both finding the right material to spray into clouds and how they do it.

Augustus Doricko, the founder and CEO of Rainmaker, is quick to answer any questions on the consequences of how his company uses the silver iodide compound. It's clear he's been asked about chemical safety many times.

He says Rainmaker releases this form of silver at 20 grams per flight, distributed across thousands of square kilometres. "The resultant increase in concentration on the ground is in the parts per quadrillion, way below the threshold laid out by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] on what is allowable."

Rainmaker's flights use drones to soar into clouds because without clouds, "we can't do anything," he says, pointing to one of the key limits of cloud-seeding processes. Cloud-seeding sessions have to wait for clouds to form to try to coax them into precipitation.

Their drones are outfitted with silver iodide flairs, and when lit the burning atomizes the water particles into a small enough size so they can stay suspended in the freezing cloud for hours, eventually turning into crystals and later rain.

Rainmaker operates in states such as Idaho, Utah, Colorado and areas of the Middle East such as Jordan. Doricko says, "Jordan residents often only have water for hours per week from their utility because of how scarce water is, and it's a privilege to try to help this storied region."

Cloud seeding's roots began in 1946 when researchers from the General Electric Research Laboratory used dry ice as the first seeding agent. A year later, silver iodide was found to be more effective than dry ice, which quickly turns into useless gas.

While seeding agents caused more rainfall, they didn't move the needle much. In fact, sobering statistics point to how patchy this technology can be in what it pours on the ground.

"With the right conditions, cloud seeding squeeze out about an extra five to 10% of precipitation," says Jon Meyer, an assistant state climatologist with the Utah Climate Center.

What was encouraging, though, for the cloud-seeding sector was a landmark 2017 study that found how silver iodide worked as expected, one of the first reports to observe cloud seeding in action using radar and precipitation gauges.

In the past several years, Meyer has been encouraged to see more companies such as Rainmaker bring innovation to an old industry. "Drones [such as Rainmaker's products] present this new avenue," says Meyer, "and they offer a more targeted nature to these clouds we hope will be responsive."

What is sprayed into clouds may also be undergoing a major shift. Recast Systems in San Francisco is experimenting with a type of protein made from amino acids found in the soil, says CEO Olivia Li.

While still undergoing tests at Texas A&M University, this new seeding agent moves Recast away from silver iodide as the go-to compound.

"It's safe, biodegradable and nucleates ice at a higher efficiency than silver iodide," says Li, whose company currently uses silver iodide to seed clouds in several US states.

Meyer is optimistic this technology's trajectory will only continue to rise. "We're going to see more demand for these services as so many regions are experiencing water demand," he says, "and they're going to be looking for ways to help bridge that gap."

articles.title: “I was so scared”: Shriya Saran recalls eve-teasing in college days; the one thing she wants daughter Radha to know and lessons parents can take home
articles.summary: When children come home after school, college, a playdate or an outing, parents often ask the same questions: “What did you do?” “Did you fight with
articles.body: When children come home after school, college, a playdate or an outing, parents often ask the same questions: “What did you do?” “Did you fight with anyone?” “Did you misbehave?” But actor Shriya Saran believes parents should also ask a different kind of question: “Did something happen to you?” Speaking in a conversation with Hauterrfly, Shriya spoke about her own experiences growing up, situations that made her feel helpless and why she believes children need to know that they can tell their parents when something uncomfortable happens to them. Her point was not simply about teaching children safe and unsafe touch. She also spoke about what happens after children have been taught about safety, particularly when they are frightened, confused or worried that they might be blamed.“We don't ask them, did something happen to you?”Shriya said parents often approach conversations with children by first checking what the child might have done wrong. “Because when children come home, we ask them, ‘Did you fight with anyone? What did you do? Did you misbehave?’ We don't ask them, ‘Did something happen to you? Did someone do something to you?’ Because we assume our children might have done something wrong,” she said.According to Shriya, this can affect how children interpret an uncomfortable experience. “That somewhere leaves an impact on children. They start thinking, ‘Maybe it was my fault.’” She said parents should instead ask questions that help them understand what actually happened. “So it is very important not to immediately blame them for being naughty. Ask properly. Ask, ‘Who was there? What happened? Who did what?’” For Shriya, listening to the child's version is an important part of making them feel safe enough to speak.Her own experience of feeling helplessShriya also recalled an incident from her college days that stayed with her. She said she was travelling by bus when she saw a boy troubling a girl at a crossing. “He was literally beating her horribly and removing her clothes. I was shocked that nobody said anything. No one around her was coming to help her,” she said. Shriya got off the bus and went towards the girl, but she was frightened herself. “So I got down from the bus. I still remember going up to her, but I was so scared that I could not do anything. My friends told me that there was no police officer around at that time, nothing. That moment left me feeling very helpless.”She said the incident continued to affect her after she returned home. “I cried a lot later at home. I remember thinking that I could not do anything at that time.” She also spoke about facing eve-teasing while travelling by bus at night during her younger years. “I loved being in the theatre. I used to take a lot of taxis and buses because I travelled by bus. There was a lot of eve-teasing at night. It was very tough, but if the bus became empty, we would get scared and get off the bus because we were afraid. Those moments stayed with me. But life gives you the energy to come out of them.”Why Shriya wants parents to talk about safe and unsafe touchWhen asked what she would not want to pass on to her daughter Radha because of her own experiences, Shriya brought up the way children are now taught about safe and unsafe touch. “Today, we talk about children being taught about safe and unsafe touch, which was not there when we were growing up.” She said many children may experience something uncomfortable without immediately understanding what has happened. “Sometimes you do not even understand what happened. Someone touched you or did something, and you did not understand it. So I think almost everyone has had some kind of bad experience.”She added, “I am glad that we now talk about these things.” But according to Shriya, simply teaching children the concept is not enough. “Even after teaching children, they still get scared. They do not speak or tell anyone. They think that maybe it was their fault and start blaming themselves.” This is where she believes the parent's response becomes particularly important.Watch for changes, not just answersShriya said parents should pay attention not only to what children say but also to changes in their behaviour. “Their reactions will tell you something. Their body language can change. It is very important to see whether their warning language is changing. Are they becoming self-conscious? Are they becoming conscious around that person? Have they suddenly become introverted?” She described these as things parents need to “really check and understand.” “Sometimes even one bad touch can really leave a scar.” She said parents cannot control every situation their children may encounter, but they can make sure children know where to turn when something happens.“We can protect children as much as we can, but beyond that, it is very important that we ask them the right questions.” “And if we feel that something is wrong, we need to take the right steps so that they feel for life that we are protecting them. Then they will be less afraid to tell you if something happens later. I think that is very important.”A small parenting shift: ask two questions, not oneOne practical change parents can make is to add a second question to the usual “What did you do today?” Instead of stopping at “What happened?”, also ask “What happened to you?” The difference is small but important. The first question can focus on the child's actions. The second gives them space to talk about something another person may have said or done to them. Parents can also make the conversation more specific without turning it into an interrogation: Who were you with? How did you feel? Did anyone make you uncomfortable? Did anything happen that you didn't understand?If a child becomes unusually quiet, avoids a particular person, suddenly becomes uncomfortable in a familiar setting or shows a noticeable change in behaviour, the first response does not have to be questioning about what the child did wrong. Listening calmly can help parents understand what the child is actually trying to communicate.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: 'Birthday gift to Putin': Russia launches massive strikes on Ukraine; energy sites hit
articles.summary: Russia’s defence ministry said on Wednesday that its forces carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and several other
articles.body: Russia’s defence ministry said on Wednesday that its forces carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and several other Ukrainian regions using high-precision weapons and drones.The ministry said the strikes involved land-, sea- and air-launched weapons as well as drones. It said targets included facilities operated by Fire Point in Kyiv, where Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones are allegedly manufactured and stored.According to the ministry, strikes also hit military-industrial sites in the Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkiv regions, according to Reuters. Eleven killed in attackAround 70 missiles along with drones were fired targeting the country’s energy infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, Reuters reported.At least 11 people were killed in the strikes across Ukraine. He described energy infrastructure as one of the main targets, accusing Russia of seeking to inflict heavy damage and send a message through the attack.“One of the key targets was our energy infrastructure. The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” Zelenskiy said in a post on Telegram.He said Russian ballistic missiles remained Ukraine’s “greatest challenge” and called for additional air defence systems, saying they were a “vital necessity” for the country.You use AI every day. articles.title: A ticketing company has sent US$13.8 million in profits to charity instead of shareholders; Hugh Jackman joined Humanitix in 2026 to help expand the model
articles.summary: A ticket booking fee can help fund more than an event.
articles.body: A ticket booking fee can help fund more than an event. Humanitix, a not-for-profit ticketing platform, says it has directed US$13.8 million in profits to charitable causes, supporting work in education, healthcare, poverty alleviation and other areas. The company's current 2026 Impact Report puts the detailed total at US$13,822,038. Actor Hugh Jackman joined Humanitix as its Head of Impact in April 2026, several years after the organisation began directing profits to charity. In his own announcement, Jackman said he wanted to “help build” the organisation rather than support it from the sidelines. Humanitix says its model dedicates 100% of the profits from its booking fees to charity, while the fees themselves help cover the costs of running the ticketing platform.How Humanitix turns booking fees into charitable givingHumanitix charges a booking fee on paid tickets sold through its platform. According to its current fee guidance, the fee covers payment-processing and merchant costs when an event uses Humanitix's own payment gateway, as well as the company's staff, servers and other tools used to operate the platform. The company says 100% of the profit generated from those fees is donated. The payment-processing arrangement is not identical for every event. Humanitix says its own payment gateway covers payment-processing costs within the booking fee, while events that use Stripe as their payment gateway incur Stripe's processing fees separately. The company also says booking fees are normally passed on to ticket buyers, although event organisers can choose to absorb them.Humanitix describes itself as a registered charity and not-for-profit organisation. It says it has no shareholders and does not pay dividends to investors. Its 2025 explanation of its donation model says revenue from booking fees is pooled with operating costs to determine how much can be donated to partner charities. That means the amount generated by an individual event cannot simply be equated with a fixed portion of its booking fees.Where the US$13.8 million has goneHumanitix's 2026 Impact Report provides a breakdown of the profits it says it has distributed. Poverty alleviation accounts for 39.74%, or US$5,492,240.57, while education accounts for 36.97%, or US$5,109,863.55. Healthcare represents 17.18%, or US$2,375,092.19. A further 4.2%, or US$580,708.13, is listed under support for Indigenous groups. The remaining 1.91%, or US$264,133.56, is categorised as other giving, including environmental and human-rights causes. The figures are published directly in Humanitix's 2026 Impact Report.The report lists a broader set of areas supported through Humanitix's charitable programme, including food security, safety and dignity, the environment, children and youth services and what the company calls life's basic necessities. Its listed charity partners include The Life You Can Save, GiveDirectly, Room to Read, Educate Girls, Food 4 Education, Healthy Learners and other organisations working in education, healthcare and poverty alleviation. Humanitix's descriptions of individual partners give examples of the work supported. Food 4 Education, for example, provides school meals in Kenya, while Healthy Learners works with the Zambian government on school-based healthcare. Educate Girls works in rural India to support girls' education, and Room to Read focuses on literacy and girls' education in low-income communities. These descriptions come from Humanitix's own partner listings rather than independent assessments of the organisations' overall effectiveness.Hugh Jackman's role at HumanitixIn a letter dated April 21, 2026, Jackman announced his appointment as Humanitix's Head of Impact. In his letter published by Humanitix, he explained that the more he learned about the organisation, the more he wanted to become involved in building it. Jackman also described Humanitix's model as different from a conventional company that makes money and later donates a portion to charity. He wrote that the organisation directs its profits towards its mission and said the model was the reason he wanted to take an active role.At the time of his appointment, Jackman wrote that Humanitix had collectively directed more than A$20 million towards projects addressing global poverty and education. Humanitix's current Australian-facing pages display a more precise Australian-dollar figure of A$20,796,400, while the US impact materials give the detailed total as US$13,822,038. The figures are different currency expressions of the reported donation total, not separate amounts that should be added together. Jackman's appointment therefore came after the organisation had already accumulated most of the reported giving. His stated role is to help build Humanitix's impact as the organisation continues its work.Humanitix also reports discounted support for non-profitsThe company's charitable model extends beyond direct donations. Humanitix offers eligible charities, schools and other non-profit organisations a discounted booking-fee rate. Its 2026 Impact Report says eligible organisations have used the discounted rate to run more than 300,000 events. The US version of the report puts the value of these discounted services at US$10.33 million and describes them as in-kind donations. Because Humanitix publishes different currency figures on different regional versions of its site, this article uses the US report's figure rather than attempting to convert or reconcile the regional amounts independently.The report also says Humanitix employees received a portion of the company's profit pool over the past 3 years and were able to direct those funds to charities of their choice. Humanitix puts the total of these staff-directed donations at US$991,853. The report does not separately state whether that amount is included within or additional to the US$13.8 million headline donation figure, so the two figures should not be combined.A ticketing business built around its profitsHumanitix's model is ultimately based on using a commercial ticketing service to generate profits for charitable giving. The company says its booking fees contribute towards operating the platform, while all profit generated from those fees is directed towards its charitable mission. Its current impact report says more than US$13.8 million has been donated to charity and identifies education, poverty alleviation and healthcare as its largest reported areas of giving. The report also identifies food security, environmental protection, support for Indigenous groups, safety and dignity, and children's services among the causes it supports.Jackman joined the organisation in 2026 with the stated aim of helping build that model. His appointment came after years of charitable giving by Humanitix, meaning the US$13.8 million figure reflects the organisation's accumulated impact rather than donations generated during Jackman's tenure. For ticket buyers, the company's proposition is straightforward: the booking fee attached to an event can contribute to a business whose profits are directed towards charitable causes rather than shareholders.You use AI every day. articles.title: Who is Vivek Bhagat?: What is the controversy around the Delhi Police officer
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police officer ACP Vivek Bhagat, currently posted as sub-divisional police officer (SDPO) in Connaught Place, has come under scrutiny
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police officer ACP Vivek Bhagat, currently posted as sub-divisional police officer (SDPO) in Connaught Place, has come under scrutiny after three women journalists alleged sexual harassment by police personnel during a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.The complaints were transferred to the Delhi Police Crime Branch for a “fair and impartial” enquiry. Bhagat has since consented to keeping his current duty charge as additional deputy commissioner of police on hold pending the enquiry.Who is Vivek Bhagat?Bhagat is a Delhi Police officer currently serving as SDPO, Connaught Place. He was among 12 Selection Grade DANIPS officers assigned the current duty charge of Additional DCP in an order approved by Lieutenant Governor Taranjit Singh Sandhu.The Delhi government later modified the order after Bhagat formally requested that the charge concerning him be kept on hold, citing the pending Crime Branch enquiry.Bhagat had also been involved in police action during protests in June, when he was injured amid clashes between protesters and police.During those protests Bhagat said that he was allegedly surrounded and overpowered during the clashes and was beaten, kicked and punched. He reported alleged head injuries, bruises and broken teeth.An ANI report from the time said Bhagat was injured by stone and bottle pelting near Tolstoy Marg. The injuries were sustained while police were dealing with protesters during the June clashes.What are the allegations against him?Three women journalists complained of sexual harassment following a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Jantar Mantar on October 3.One journalist specifically alleged that Bhagat sexually assaulted her while she was covering the protest. She said she had approached him after noticing that no women police personnel were present while protesters were being detained.According to her complaint, she asked Bhagat about the absence of women personnel, following which he allegedly sexually assaulted and pushed her.The allegations have not been established. The Delhi Police transferred the complaints to its Crime Branch, which is examining the allegations and recording statements of the complainants and other people concerned.Why is his promotion controversial?The allegations emerged just days before Bhagat was among 12 officers assigned the current duty charge of Additional DCP.A senior police officer said the promotions were routine and that the request for the promotions had been sent much earlier.After the allegations and the pending enquiry came to light, Bhagat wrote to the Delhi Police Commissioner saying he consented to keeping the order concerning him on hold until the enquiry was dealt with.The Delhi government subsequently modified the administrative order, putting his Additional DCP charge on hold.The Crime Branch enquiry will determine the facts surrounding the allegations. The complaints remain allegations at this stage, and the material available does not establish that Bhagat committed sexual harassment.The Press Council of India has meanwhile expressed “shock and dismay” over the allegations and urged Delhi Police to act on the journalists’ complaints, saying journalists must be able to work without facing aggression or threats.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
